title: Definition and focus areas of macroeconomics revisited
competency: Define macroeconomics, explain its focus areas, goals and variables, and distinguish GDP from GNP.

keywords.def: The study of the decisions of individual economic units — households, firms, governments — at a disaggregated level.
The study of the economy as a whole: overall output, prices and employment, and the policies that affect them.
Economy-wide targets: economic growth, full employment, price stability, lower budget or balance-of-payments deficits, fair income distribution.
Measures that show the state and trend of the whole economy, e.g. GDP, GNP, inflation, unemployment, exports, exchange rate.
Gross domestic product: the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country during a year. GDP = Σ Pᵢ Qᵢ.
Gross national product: the value of final goods and services produced by a country's own factors of production, wherever located. GNP = GDP + NFI.
NFI: factor income (wages, rent, interest, profits) received from abroad by citizens minus factor income paid to foreigners.
GDP measured in actual (current) market prices.
GDP measured in constant prices of a base year, so price changes are removed.

en.text: Microeconomics studies the decisions of individual units such as households, firms and governments. Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: total output, the general price level and employment. Macroeconomics is a relatively new branch that emerged after Keynes' General Theory (1936); "macro" comes from the Greek "makro", meaning large.

screens.title: Micro and macro
paras: Economics is divided into microeconomics and macroeconomics.
Microeconomics studies individual units: households, firms, governments.
It works at a disaggregated level.
Macroeconomics studies the overall (aggregate) behaviour of the economy.
It looks at total output, prices and employment.

It emerged after Keynes' book The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936).
"Macro" comes from the Greek "makro": large.
It studies the structure and performance of national economies.
It also studies the policies governments use to affect them.

en.text: Macroeconomics focuses on aggregate behaviour: economic growth, employment, inflation, income distribution, macroeconomic policies and international trade. Its goals are economic growth, full employment, price stability, lower budget or balance-of-payments deficits, and a fair distribution of income. Macroeconomic variables such as GDP, GNP, the growth rate, the price level, unemployment, exports, imports and the exchange rate show the state of the whole economy.

en.text: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country during a year: GDP = Σ Pᵢ Qᵢ. GNP is the value of final output produced by a country's own factors of production, wherever they are located. They are linked by GNP = GDP + NFI, where NFI is factor income received from abroad minus factor income paid to foreigners; in a closed economy NFI = 0, so GNP = GDP.

am.text: ጠቅላላ የሀገር ውስጥ ምርት በሀገሪቱ ውስጥ የተመረቱ የመጨረሻ ዕቃዎችና አገልግሎቶች ዋጋ ነው። ጠቅላላ ብሔራዊ ምርት = ጠቅላላ የሀገር ውስጥ ምርት + የተጣራ የውጭ ገቢ።

screens.title: Whose output?
screens.ask: A Chinese-owned factory in Hawassa makes shirts. In which country's GDP do the shirts count?
opts: Ethiopia's, because they are made in Ethiopia
China's, because the owner is Chinese
screens.after: GDP counts output made inside the country, whoever owns the factory. The owner's profit belongs to China's GNP.

screens.title: Gross domestic product (GDP)
paras: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country during a year.
GDP = Σ Pᵢ Qᵢ.
Pᵢ: the prices of outputs of the different sectors.
Qᵢ: the quantities of final goods and services.

screens.title: Gross national product (GNP)
paras: GNP is the value of final goods and services produced by a country's own factors of production.
It counts them wherever they are located.
GNP = GDP + NFI.
NFI = factor income received from abroad by citizens − factor income paid to foreigners.
Factor income means wages, rent, interest and profits.

screens.title: From GDP to GNP
steps: Citizens earn 30 billion abroad; foreigners earn 50 billion here.
NFI is negative, so GNP < GDP.

Gross national product: the value of final goods and services produced by a country's own factors of production, wherever located. GNP = GDP + NFI.
NFI: factor income (wages, rent, interest, profits) received from abroad by citizens minus factor income paid to foreigners.

screens.text: Many Ethiopians work abroad and earn wages there; few foreigners work in Ethiopia. Then
screens.why: Wages earned abroad by citizens are factor income received. Received > paid, so NFI > 0 and GNP > GDP.

screens.text: GNP = GDP + net transfers such as gifts and aid from other countries.
screens.why: GNP = GDP + net FACTOR income: wages, rent, interest and profits. Gifts and aid are transfers, not factor income.

screens.ask: GNP = 2,400 bn Birr and NFI = −60 bn Birr. GDP = ___ bn Birr
screens.why: GDP = GNP − NFI = 2,400 − (−60) = 2,460 bn Birr.
screens.clue: Rearrange GNP = GDP + NFI.

ideas.name: Measuring GDP: three approaches, nominal and real

en.text: GDP can be measured by the product (value-added) approach, the expenditure approach and the income approach. The expenditure approach adds consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports: GDP = C + I + G + NE, with NE = X − M. Nominal GDP uses current market prices; real GDP uses constant base-year prices, so its changes show real output growth.

am.text: ጠቅላላ የሀገር ውስጥ ምርት በምርት፣ በወጪ እና በገቢ ዘዴዎች ይለካል። ስመ ምርት በወቅቱ ዋጋ፣ እውነተኛ ምርት በመሠረት ዓመት ዋጋ ይሰላል።

screens.title: Counting bread
screens.ask: A farmer sells wheat to a miller for 60 Birr. The miller sells flour to a baker for 100 Birr. The baker sells bread for 150 Birr. How much should GDP count?
screens.after: Wheat and flour are used up in the bread; counting them again is double counting. Value added: 60 + 40 + 50 = 150 Birr.

screens.title: Three approaches
paras: Product (value-added) approach: add the market value produced by each sector.
Count final goods only, to avoid double counting.
Expenditure approach: add all spending on final goods and services.
GDP = C + I + G + NE.
C: household consumption. I: private investment. G: government purchases. NE: net exports = X − M.
Income approach: add incomes of factor owners: wages and salaries, rent, interest, profits.
Add other claims on output, less subsidies and transfer payments.

screens.title: Nominal and real GDP
paras: Nominal GDP uses actual (current) market prices.
Real GDP uses constant prices of a base year.
Real GDP removes the effect of price changes.
Changes in real GDP are the most widely used measure of output and growth.

screens.title: Nominal versus real
steps: Year 1 (base): 100 units at 10 Birr. Nominal = real = 1,000 Birr.
Year 2: 110 units at 12 Birr. Nominal = 110 × 12 = 1,320 Birr.
Nominal growth = 32 %: most of it is price increase.

screens.ask: A farm sells 50 bags at 20 Birr (base year), and 50 bags at 30 Birr the next year. Real GDP growth = ___ %
screens.why: Real GDP both years = 50 × 20 = 1,000 Birr, so real growth = 0 %. Nominal GDP rose only because the price rose.
screens.clue: Value both years at base-year prices.

screens.text: Nominal GDP rose 20 % while prices also rose about 20 %. What happened to real GDP?
screens.why: Real growth ≈ nominal growth − price rise = 20 − 20 = 0. All of the rise was prices.
screens.clue: Remove the price effect.

notes.text: Table 1.1 (p.4): "Gross domestic production" should be "Gross domestic product" and "Per capital income" should be "Per capita income"; the two right-hand columns are one list of variables, not pairs. The lesson shows the variables beside their focus areas.
p.4–5: GNP is said to be GDP "plus transfers to/from other countries". It is GDP + net FACTOR income (wages, rent, interest, profits), not transfers; the lesson teaches GNP = GDP + NFI.
p.5: "counties" should be "countries". Real GNP corrects for price changes over time; comparing price levels across countries needs PPP adjustment.
Worked illustrations (teff/shirts GDP, GDP→GNP, expenditure approach, nominal vs real, bread value added, Hawassa factory) are added; the book has no worked GDP examples.
